title: Ventricular Tachyarrhythmia in a Newborn Baby
case_prompt:
A female infant was born at 37 weeks’ gestation to a gravida 3 para 1 mother with no medical history and negative maternal labs. At birth, her heart rate was consistently above 200 beats per minute. APGAR scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. Physical examination was unremarkable except for a 4 cm × 4 cm blanching hemangioma on the back. 

In the neonatal ICU, ECG showed a heart rate of 235 bpm, broad QRS tachycardia with P waves following the QRS complexes, and possible delta waves. Vagal maneuvers and escalating doses of IV adenosine failed to terminate the tachycardia, so synchronized cardioversion restored sinus rhythm. The infant was started on an IV procainamide infusion and oral propranolol; procainamide was discontinued after 24 hours. 

The ECG continued to show wide‐complex tachycardia, and the initial differential included VT versus SVT with aberrant conduction. Assuming SVT, vagal maneuvers and adenosine were repeated; adenosine produced 1:1 conduction with no AV dissociation but did not terminate the tachycardia, necessitating another cardioversion. 

On day 2, multiple recurrences of wide‐complex tachycardia at ~200 bpm occurred, all resistant to adenosine and treated with cardioversion twice more. Propranolol was increased, and IV procainamide was replaced with IV amiodarone. On day 3, ECG again showed wide QRS tachycardia at 170 bpm, which resolved spontaneously on day 9 of life. Transthoracic echocardiography during admission showed no cardiomegaly or intracardiac masses.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. SVT with aberrant conduction was initially presumed because SVT is more common in neonates — “Since SVT is more common in neonates, the initial treatment approach assumed that the tachyarrhythmia was SVT.”  
2. The response to adenosine showed 1:1 conduction without AV dissociation, supporting SVT — “Administration of Adenosine showed 1:1 conduction with no evidence of atrio-ventricular dissociation; this finding is consistent with SVT.”  
3. Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome was considered due to baseline pre-excitation on ECG — “baseline EKG shortly after birth showed a shortened PR interval in lead V2, suggesting ventricular pre-excitation at baseline (WPW syndrome).”  
4. VT was considered given the wide QRS, recurrent tachycardia, and failure to convert with adenosine — “Due to failure to convert her tachyarrhythmia with Adenosine and repeated need for conversion, our patient’s tachyarrhythmia was likely ventricular in origin.”  
5. Structural and metabolic causes of VT (tumors, congenital heart disease, myocarditis, long QT syndrome, electrolyte abnormalities) were excluded by normal echocardiogram and laboratory results — “Causes of ventricular tachycardia include cardiac tumors, congenital heart disease, myocarditis, long QT syndrome and electrolyte abnormalities, none of which our patient was found to have.”
